triage.reason: Malabsorption case with a clear diagnosis reachable by history, exam, serology and biopsy, plus important look-alikes.

demographics: More common in people of European descent, especially Northern European ancestry
Can occur in any ethnic group
More common in females than males

risk_factors.text: Down syndrome, Turner syndrome, or Williams syndrome

family_history: Celiac disease in a first-degree relative
exposures: Diet containing wheat, barley, or rye

chief_complaints.text: I've been having diarrhea for months
I feel tired all the time
My stomach is always bloated and gassy
I have an itchy, blistery rash

hpi.onset: Gradual, often over weeks to months; may follow a viral illness, pregnancy, or stress
hpi.duration: Chronic, usually months to years before diagnosis
hpi.progression: Persistent or intermittent symptoms that wax and wane; slowly progressive malabsorption if untreated
hpi.location: Diffuse abdominal discomfort, often periumbilical or generalized
hpi.quality: Crampy abdominal pain with bloating and loose stools
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; can become severe with significant weight loss and malnutrition
hpi.timing: Related to meals; diarrhea often worse after eating gluten-containing foods

associated_symptoms.text: Chronic diarrhea or greasy, bulky, foul-smelling stools

pertinent_negatives: Severe weight loss with night sweats
Travel to areas with poor sanitation

positives.text: Itchy blistering rash on elbows, knees, or buttocks

atypical.how_it_differs: Children often present with failure to thrive, poor weight gain, irritability, and digestive symptoms; extraintestinal symptoms are less common.
May present with anemia, osteoporosis, or neuropathy without prominent diarrhea.
May present with anemia, fatigue, and recurrent miscarriage; symptoms may be attributed to pregnancy.

general.mild: Well-appearing, no distress; may look tired
general.moderate: Thin, pale, mildly fatigued but not toxic
general.severe: Cachectic or visibly malnourished, pale, weak, ill-appearing

findings.maneuver: Measure weight and compare with prior records or reported usual weight; calculate BMI
findings.finding: Unintentional weight loss or low BMI

findings.maneuver: Plot height, weight, and BMI on a growth chart in a child
Inspect the conjunctivae and palmar creases
findings.finding: Conjunctival or palmar pallor suggesting anemia
Mild diffuse or periumbilical tenderness without focal or rebound tenderness
No hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, or abdominal mass

findings.maneuver: Inspect the extensor surfaces of the elbows and knees, the buttocks, and the scalp
findings.finding: Intensely itchy grouped vesicles or excoriated papules on an erythematous base (dermatitis herpetiformis)

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lips and oral mucosa
findings.finding: Angular cheilitis or cracking at the mouth corners

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oral mucosa and tongue
findings.finding: Recurrent aphthous ulcers or a smooth, atrophic tongue

findings.maneuver: Test vibration, pinprick, and light touch in the feet
findings.finding: Reduced distal sensation suggesting peripheral neuropathy

findings.maneuver: Perform a digital rectal exam when bleeding or malignancy is a concern

labs.caveat: Iron-deficiency anemia is the most common laboratory clue; anemia may be absent in mild or screen-detected disease.
Microcytic from iron deficiency; can be normocytic or macrocytic when folate or B12 deficiency coexists.
Low ferritin confirms iron deficiency; ferritin is an acute-phase reactant and may look normal when inflammation is present.
Elevated TIBC with low iron and low ferritin supports iron deficiency.
Low folate from malabsorption; can cause a macrocytic anemia.
Low B12 from terminal ileal malabsorption; contributes to anemia and neuropathy.
Low albumin reflects protein malabsorption and chronic inflammation; a low value supports more severe disease.
Hypocalcemia from vitamin D and calcium malabsorption; check albumin because total calcium falls with low albumin.
Elevated alkaline phosphatase can reflect osteomalacia or secondary hyperparathyroidism from malabsorption.
Ordered to look for associated autoimmune thyroid disease; an elevated TSH suggests hypothyroidism.

imaging.study: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with duodenal biopsy
imaging.preferred_when: All patients being evaluated for celiac disease while still eating gluten

findings.text: Scalloping or loss of the normal duodenal fold pattern
Attenuation or flattening of duodenal folds
Normal-appearing duodenal mucosa (visible appearance does not exclude disease)
Flocculation or clumping of barium from increased intraluminal fluid
Loss of the normal feathery fold pattern

imaging.preferred_when: Adults at diagnosis and those with malabsorption or fracture risk

findings.text: Low bone mineral density (osteopenia or osteoporosis)

initial.why: Looks for anemia and microcytosis from iron deficiency
Assesses albumin, calcium, and alkaline phosphatase as markers of malabsorption
Confirms iron deficiency and checks folate and vitamin B12
Screens for associated autoimmune thyroid disease
First-line serology for celiac disease while the patient is still eating gluten
Detects IgA deficiency, which can cause a false-negative IgA tissue transglutaminase result

confirmatory.test: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with duodenal biopsy
confirmatory.why: Shows villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes; the reference standard for diagnosis

supporting.why: Highly specific serology used when tissue transglutaminase is equivocal or discordant
Less specific; occasionally used in young children or when other serology is unavailable
High negative predictive value; a negative result makes celiac disease very unlikely
supporting.only_if: serology and biopsy are discordant or the diagnosis is uncertain
adult at diagnosis or with malabsorption

not_indicated.why: Nonspecific; celiac disease does not typically cause marked systemic inflammation
Nonspecific and not part of the diagnostic workup
Not needed unless pancreatitis is suspected
No role in chronic diarrhea or malabsorption
Urinary infection does not explain chronic diarrhea and weight loss
Rarely changes management now that serology and biopsy are available
not_indicated.only_if: endoscopy is not possible or a structural small bowel lesion is suspected

not_indicated.why: Not a routine diagnostic test because these alleles are common in the general population
not_indicated.only_if: serology and biopsy are discordant or the diagnosis is uncertain

decision_points: Serology and biopsy must be obtained while the patient is still eating gluten; a gluten-free diet before testing causes false-negative results
Check total IgA when tissue transglutaminase IgA is negative or borderline, because IgA deficiency can cause a false-negative result
Do not start a gluten-free diet before the diagnostic workup is complete
Consider HLA-DQ2/DQ8 testing only when serology and biopsy disagree

criteria.name: Celiac disease diagnosis
criteria.summary: Diagnosis requires compatible history and examination plus positive celiac serology and characteristic duodenal biopsy findings while the patient is on a gluten-containing diet. In selected children with very high tissue transglutaminase levels, some guidelines allow diagnosis without biopsy after discussion with a specialist.
items: Symptoms or risk factors suggesting celiac disease
Positive IgA tissue transglutaminase (with normal total IgA) or positive endomysial antibody
Duodenal biopsy showing villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes
Testing performed while the patient is eating gluten

differential.name: Irritable bowel syndrome
differential.why_considered: Chronic bloating, abdominal pain, and altered stool habits are common to both conditions

history: Pain relieved by defecation and linked to stool frequency or form
No weight loss, anemia, or greasy foul-smelling stools
Symptoms fluctuate for years without progressive malnutrition
exam: Normal general appearance and nutritional status
Mild diffuse tenderness without distention or pallor
labs: Normal hemoglobin, ferritin, albumin, and folate

differential.name: Inflammatory bowel disease
differential.why_considered: Chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, and weight loss can suggest Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis
differential.trigger: Bloody diarrhea, nocturnal symptoms, fever, or perianal disease

history: Bloody or mucoid diarrhea
Nocturnal diarrhea that wakes the patient
Fever, night sweats, or perianal fistulas
Family history of inflammatory bowel disease
exam: Focal abdominal tenderness or a right lower quadrant mass
Aphthous ulcers and erythema nodosum or pyoderma gangrenosum
imaging: Terminal ileum thickening or skip lesions on CT or MRI enterography
Mucosal ulceration and inflammation on colonoscopy

differential.name: Lactose intolerance
differential.why_considered: Bloating, gas, and diarrhea after dairy are common in celiac disease and in primary lactose intolerance

history: Symptoms occur only after milk or dairy, not after wheat, barley, or rye
No weight loss, anemia, or extraintestinal features
Symptoms improve promptly with lactose avoidance
exam: Normal nutritional status and no rash
labs: Positive hydrogen breath test after lactose load

differential.name: Wheat allergy
differential.why_considered: Symptoms after eating wheat can be mistaken for celiac disease
differential.trigger: Urticaria, wheezing, or hypotension shortly after wheat ingestion

history: Rapid onset within minutes to hours of wheat ingestion
Itchy eyes, hives, lip swelling, or trouble breathing
No chronic diarrhea or malabsorption

differential.name: Non-celiac gluten sensitivity
differential.why_considered: Gluten-related bloating, fatigue, and abdominal pain without villous atrophy

history: Symptoms improve on a gluten-free diet but no malabsorption
No weight loss, anemia, or dermatitis herpetiformis
labs: Negative tissue transglutaminase IgA and endomysial antibody
Normal duodenal biopsy while on gluten

differential.name: Tropical sprue
differential.why_considered: Chronic diarrhea, weight loss, and malabsorption with small bowel mucosal injury

history: Residence or travel in the tropics
Symptoms persist despite a gluten-free diet
Often responds to antibiotics and folate
exam: Signs of folate or B12 deficiency
labs: Megaloblastic anemia with low folate or B12
imaging: Small bowel biopsy shows villous atrophy but no response to gluten withdrawal

differential.name: Whipple disease
differential.why_considered: Malabsorption with weight loss, diarrhea, and systemic symptoms
differential.trigger: Arthralgias, fever, and neurologic or cardiac findings with malabsorption

history: Migratory arthralgias and arthritis
Fever, night sweats, and lymphadenopathy
Neurologic symptoms such as memory problems or ophthalmoplegia
labs: PCR or biopsy showing Tropheryma whipplei
imaging: Small bowel biopsy with PAS-positive macrophages

differential.name: Giardiasis
differential.why_considered: Chronic diarrhea, bloating, and malabsorption after exposure to contaminated water

history: Recent travel or camping with untreated water
Acute onset of watery diarrhea followed by weeks of bloating
No dermatitis herpetiformis
labs: Stool microscopy or antigen positive for Giardia
imaging: Normal duodenal biopsy or trophozoites seen on biopsy

differential.name: Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth
differential.why_considered: Bloating, diarrhea, and malabsorption from bacterial overgrowth

history: Prior abdominal surgery, stricture, or motility disorder
Symptoms may improve with antibiotics
No gluten-dependent pattern
labs: Positive hydrogen or methane breath test
imaging: Normal duodenal biopsy or nonspecific inflammation

severity.mild: Subtle or intermittent symptoms such as bloating, fatigue, or mild diarrhea; anemia may be the only laboratory clue; no significant weight loss or nutritional deficiency
severity.moderate: Persistent diarrhea, abdominal pain, and bloating with weight loss, iron-deficiency anemia, or low albumin; daily activities affected
severity.severe: Marked weight loss, cachexia, hypoalbuminemia, hypocalcemia, multiple vitamin deficiencies, and bone loss; may require hospitalization for nutritional support
severity.critical: Rare life-threatening presentations such as severe dehydration, electrolyte derangement, or refeeding syndrome after prolonged starvation; untreated celiac crisis with profound malnutrition

red_flags.finding: Bloody diarrhea or nocturnal diarrhea waking from sleep
red_flags.meaning: Suggests inflammatory bowel disease or another cause rather than uncomplicated celiac disease
Raises concern for infection, lymphoma, or Whipple disease

red_flags.finding: Severe weight loss with progressive weakness
red_flags.meaning: Suggests advanced malabsorption or an underlying malignancy such as enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma

red_flags.finding: Hypotension, tachycardia, or decreased urine output
red_flags.meaning: Dehydration or severe malnutrition requiring urgent fluid and electrolyte management

red_flags.finding: Persistent symptoms despite a strict gluten-free diet
red_flags.meaning: Consider refractory celiac disease, inadvertent gluten exposure, or an alternative diagnosis

complications.name: Osteoporosis and osteomalacia
clues: Low bone mineral density on DXA
Low calcium and elevated alkaline phosphatase

complications.name: Peripheral neuropathy
clues: Numbness or tingling in the feet

complications.name: Enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma
clues: Worsening symptoms despite a gluten-free diet
Weight loss, fever, and abdominal pain
Small bowel mass or ulceration on imaging

complications.name: Refractory celiac disease
clues: Persistent villous atrophy and symptoms after at least 12 months of strict gluten-free diet

special_populations.differences: Often present with failure to thrive, poor weight gain, irritability, and digestive symptoms; growth charts are essential; extraintestinal symptoms are less common.
May present with anemia, osteoporosis, or neuropathy without prominent diarrhea; higher risk of bone loss and nutritional deficiency.
May present with anemia, fatigue, and recurrent miscarriage; symptoms may be attributed to pregnancy; untreated disease increases risk of low birth weight and preterm delivery.

key_questions.question: What do your stools look like — are they loose, greasy, bulky, or unusually foul-smelling?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic diarrhea or steatorrhea, the classic malabsorption pattern

key_questions.question: How long has this been going on, and is it constant or does it come and go?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic symptoms over months to years that wax and wane

key_questions.question: Do your symptoms get worse after eating bread, pasta, cereal, or beer?
Have you lost weight without trying, or has your appetite changed?
key_questions.looking_for: Unintentional weight loss or poor weight gain in a child

key_questions.question: Have you noticed bloating, gas, or crampy belly pain?
Do you feel tired or short of breath with activity?
key_questions.looking_for: Fatigue or exertional dyspnea suggesting anemia

key_questions.question: Have you had an itchy, blistery rash on your elbows, knees, or buttocks?
Do you get mouth sores, or does your tongue feel sore or smooth?
key_questions.looking_for: Aphthous ulcers or atrophic glossitis from nutritional deficiency

key_questions.question: Have you had any bone or joint pain, or broken a bone easily?
key_questions.looking_for: Bone pain or fragility suggesting osteopenia or osteomalacia

key_questions.question: Do you have numbness, tingling, or balance problems in your feet?
Has anyone in your family been diagnosed with celiac disease or another autoimmune condition?
key_questions.looking_for: First-degree relative with celiac disease or associated autoimmunity

key_questions.question: Do you have type 1 diabetes, thyroid disease, or a genetic condition like Down or Turner syndrome?
key_questions.looking_for: Conditions strongly associated with celiac disease

key_questions.question: Have you already started a gluten-free diet or tried removing gluten on your own?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior gluten restriction, which can cause false-negative serology and biopsy

key_questions.question: Have you had any fevers, night sweats, or diarrhea that wakes you from sleep?
key_questions.looking_for: Features that argue against uncomplicated celiac disease and suggest infection, IBD, or malignancy

key_questions.question: Have you had trouble getting pregnant or had miscarriages?
key_questions.looking_for: Infertility or recurrent pregnancy loss associated with untreated disease

reasoning_points: Chronic diarrhea with greasy, bulky, foul-smelling stools and bloating suggesting malabsorption
Unintentional weight loss, fatigue, or iron-deficiency anemia
Symptoms provoked by gluten-containing foods and relieved by gluten avoidance
Associated autoimmune or genetic conditions such as type 1 diabetes, thyroid disease, Down syndrome, or Turner syndrome
Family history of celiac disease in a first-degree relative
Dermatitis herpetiformis on extensor surfaces supports the diagnosis
Positive IgA tissue transglutaminase with a normal total IgA, or positive endomysial antibody
Duodenal biopsy showing villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes
Testing performed while the patient is still eating gluten, since a gluten-free diet causes false-negative results
Alternative causes of chronic diarrhea and malabsorption considered and excluded

easy: Young adult or child with chronic diarrhea, bloating, and weight loss
Symptoms clearly worse after wheat, barley, or rye
Iron-deficiency anemia and low albumin on labs
medium: Adult with anemia or osteoporosis but little or no diarrhea
Itchy blistering rash on elbows and knees without prominent GI symptoms
Symptoms attributed to irritable bowel syndrome for years
Associated type 1 diabetes or autoimmune thyroid disease
IgA deficiency making the usual serology falsely negative
hard: Older adult presenting only with neuropathy or bone loss
Patient already eating gluten-free, causing negative serology and biopsy
Child with failure to thrive and irritability but no classic diarrhea
Pregnant patient with anemia and recurrent miscarriage
Persistent symptoms despite a strict gluten-free diet, raising concern for refractory disease or lymphoma
